title: Edward the Black Prince
description: Heir apparent of Edward III of England (1330–1376)
wiki_lead:
Edward of Woodstock (15 June 1330 – 8 June 1376), known as the Black Prince, was the eldest son and heir apparent of King Edward III of England. He died before his father, and his son Richard II therefore succeeded to the throne instead. Edward was one of the most successful English commanders of the Hundred Years' War (1337–1453). He was regarded by English contemporaries as a model of chivalry and one of the greatest knights of his era, while French sources remember him for his brutality. 
Edward was made Duke of Cornwall, the first English dukedom, in 1337. He was made Prince of Wales in 1343, and knighted by his father at La Hougue in 1346. That same year, Edward commanded the vanguard at the Battle of Crécy. He took part in Edward III's 1349 Calais expedition. In 1355, he was appointed the king's lieutenant in Gascony, and ordered to lead an army into Aquitaine on a chevauchée, during which he sacked Avignonet, Castelnaudary, Carcassonne, and Narbonne. In 1356, on another chevauchée, he ravaged Auvergne, Limousin, and Berry, though he failed to take Bourges. The forces of King John II of France met Edward's army near the city of Poitiers. After negotiations between them broke down, the Battle of Poitiers began. Edward's forces routed the French army and captured John II.
In 1360, he negotiated the Treaty of Brétigny. He was made Prince of Aquitaine and Gascony in 1362, but his suzerainty was not recognised by the Lord of Albret or other Gascon nobles. He was directed by his father in 1364 to suppress raids of the English and Gascon free companies. He made an agreement with Kings Peter of Castile and Charles II of Navarre, by which Peter covenanted to mortgage Castro Urdiales and the province of Biscay to him as security for a loan; in 1366, a passage was secured through Navarre. In 1367, he defeated Henry of Trastámara, Peter's half-brother and rival, at the Battle of Nájera. After waiting several months—during which, he failed to obtain either the province of Biscay, or liquidation of the debt from Don Pedro—he returned to Aquitaine. Edward persuaded the estates of Aquitaine to allow him a hearth tax of ten sous for five years in 1368, which alienated the Lord of Albret and other nobles.
Prince Edward returned to England in 1371 and resigned the principality of Aquitaine and Gascony in 1372. He led the Commons in their attack upon the Lancastrian administration in 1376, before dying soon after.

Early life (1330–1343)

Edward, the eldest son of Edward III of England—Lord of Ireland and ruler of Gascony, and Queen Philippa—was born at Woodstock, Oxfordshire, on 15 June 1330. On 10 September, Edward III allocated five hundred marks per year from the profits of the county of Chester to financially support his son; on 25 February 1331, the whole of these profits were assigned to the queen for supporting Edward and the king's sister Eleanor. grok_lead: Edward of Woodstock (15 June 1330 â 8 June 1376), eldest son of King Edward III of England and Queen Philippa of Hainault, served as heir apparent and a principal commander in the early phases of the Hundred Years' War against France. Created Prince of Wales in 1343 and Duke of Cornwall earlier that year, he led English longbowmen to decisive victory at the Battle of CrÃ©cy in 1346 at age sixteen, where innovative tactics routed a larger French force despite its heavy cavalry and Genoese crossbowmen. In 1356, at Poitiers, his smaller Anglo-Gascon army employed feigned retreats and archery to capture King John II of France, yielding immense ransom and prestige that prolonged English continental holdings. Appointed Prince of Aquitaine in 1362, he governed the duchy through chevauchÃ©esâraids aimed at economic devastationâbut his heavy taxation and support for the absentee Castilian pretender Pedro the Cruel alienated locals, sparking the 1369 revolt that forced his withdrawal amid failing health from dysentery or a spinal condition. Predeceasing his father in 1376, he never ascended the throne, leaving his young son Richard to succeed Edward III as Richard II. The sobriquet "Black Prince," absent from contemporary records and first attested in the sixteenth century, likely derives from his heraldic label of sable (black) or possibly the dark polish of his armor, rather than medieval chroniclers' retrospective emphasis on reputed ruthlessness in campaigns like the 1370 sack of Limoges, where civilian massacres underscored the era's total warfare norms. His chivalric Order of the Garter membership and tournament prowess contrasted with pragmatic brutality, embodying Plantagenet martial ethos amid fiscal strains from prolonged conflict that ultimately eroded English gains.
